newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends off, fails to break resistance.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends off, fails to break resistance.

text.p: NYMEX gasoline ended lower Wednesday on late session profit-taking after it was unable to break technical resistance levels following a two-day rally, traders said.
"The market needed to decide whether it was going to push gasoline through 70.00 cents or not, and at the end, it gave up on the attempt," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.
January gasoline ended 0.89 cent a gallon lower at 68.24 cents while January heating oil fell 0.65 cent a gallon to 73.57 cents. Jan crude ended off 13 cents at $24.80 a barrel.
Dealers said heat was weak on bearish weekly oil inventory data, while crude lost ground on declines in refined products.
Earlier in the session, January gasoline rose to 69.85 cents, its third consecutive contract high and just below 70.00 cents, an area of key resistance.

French unions were urging oil company workers to participate in a one-day oil industry strike on December 10, spurring gasoline's earlier gains. The unions' call comes during a strike by workers at three refineries owned by France's Elf Aquitaine that has lasted a week so far. The French unions are protesting oil industry cost cutting.
The strike at French oil giant Elf Aquitaine has crippled a quarter of French refinery capacity and three quarters of Elf's refining network in Europe, 440,000 barrels a day in capacity.
Traders said Europe will need to hold on to what gasoline supplies it has, limiting gasoline imports when U.S. gasoline supplies are also tight.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said Tuesday that distillate stocks grew 1.8 million barrels for the week ended November 29. The U.S. Energy Information Administration said Wednesday morning that its own inventory report showed distillate stocks swelled 3.9 million barrels.
Distillate stocks are comprised of heating oil and diesel. The data surprised some traders who thought stocks would decline due to higher demand fueled by recent cold weather in many U.S. regions.
-- Harry Milling, New York Enery Desk, 212-859-1761
